proposal: The chapter suggests that the high incumbency profits of large firms may come partly from regulatory capture, which can bar new entrants, and that compliance costs favor large firms that can spread them over more revenue and invest in government relations. It says the FTC must therefore consider the role of government itself in maintaining concentration in areas such as pharmaceuticals, health care, avionics, banking and real estate brokerage.

status_summary: Executive Order 14267 (signed 2025-04-09, published 2025-04-15, 90 FR 15629) directs agencies to identify regulations that create monopolies, entry barriers or limits on competition, and directs the FTC Chairman to run a public request for information and to send the Office of Management and Budget a consolidated list of regulations recommended for rescission or modification. The FTC opened its request for comment on 2025-04-13 (due 2025-05-27), and the Justice Department's Antitrust Division announced an Anticompetitive Regulations Task Force on 2025-03-27 that named housing, transportation, food and agriculture, health care and energy among its focus areas. On 2025-05-05 the FTC and DOJ sent agency heads a letter asking for lists, and on 2025-09-16 the FTC Chairman sent OMB an initial report recommending deletion or modification of over 125 regulations, with a supplemental report planned. The effort matches the chapter's call to look at government's role in concentration in part: it is an economy-wide inventory, the sampled examples (procurement, education, product safety, grazing permits) are not the sectors the chapter names, and no repeal or rule change resulting from the list was found.

timeline.event: The Justice Department announced an Antitrust Division Anticompetitive Regulations Task Force and opened a public inquiry (comments due 2025-05-27) naming housing, transportation, food and agriculture, health care and energy among focus areas.

title: FTC to weigh government's role in market concentration, including regulatory capture
uncertainties: Pages and sources were read as summaries, not as raw text. The full consolidated list was not found public; a law-firm article reports it had not been released and a House member asked OMB for it on 2025-09-30, so the sectors it covers are unknown beyond the cover letter examples. No repeal, rule or supplemental report resulting from the list was found, but searches were limited in number and absence is not proven. The executive order's date was confirmed on the Federal Register; the Task Force page was updated 2025-04-24 and the announcement date comes from that page. The chapter's concern is the FTC weighing government's role in concentration, and the order-driven inventory is counted as a partial match because the order's categories cover entry barriers and incumbent protection generally while the chapter names specific sectors. Whether the Mandate text asks for analysis in enforcement rather than deregulatory lists is a judgment call. A Federal Register search for the order title after 2025-09-17 returned only unrelated agency rules; no supplemental report, no published consolidated list and no rule resulting from it were found in the FTC press release listing, trade searches or a law-firm update. An FTC staff comment of 2026-09-22 supporting a Department of Education proposal on accreditation was found; the page does not cite the order or the phrase anticompetitive regulations, and education is not a sector named in the chapter, so it was not counted. Through 2026-10-19, absence of a later report is not proven.
